newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Eight KAL crash survivors airlifted to South Korea.
newsitem.headline: Eight KAL crash survivors airlifted to South Korea.

text.p: Eight people who miraculously survived the fiery crash of a Korean Air Lines jumbo jet on Guam were airlifted to Seoul on Friday, witnesses said.

The eight were lowered on stretchers from a U.S. medical evacuation plane to eight ambulances which sped them to hospital for treatment of injuries they suffered when Flight 801 slammed into a hillside on the Pacific island on Wednesday.
U.S. military medical personnel and Korean nurses accompanied seven South Koreans and a Korean-born American who were in a good enough state to travel to Seoul, airport officials said.
The ambulances, each with an attending doctor and a nurse, were escorted by police motocycles as they headed for four burn centres and hospitals in town.
Some of the survivors were swathed in bandages from head to foot while others had swollen faces still smeared with blood from cuts.

The military evacuation plane, C-9 Nightingale, is due to fly back to Guam to ferry 11 more South Korean survivors home, Seoul officials said. Most survivors suffered burns from a fire that broke out after the crash, KAL officials said.
U.S. officials said only 27 of 254 people aboard survived the crash. Five other people were alive when they were pulled from the smouldering wreckage, but died later in hospital.
Rescuers have given up hope of finding any more survivors amid the wreckage.
Among the eight was Park Joo-hee, a 16-year-old female student whose mother was believed to have perished in the inferno of the wreckage and who had urged rescuers not to give up search efforts.
Doctors at Guam said they did not tell the survivors of the fate of fellow passengers to avoid upsetting the patients.

"I felt like I was dying in each second of waiting amid conflicting news reports that my son died or survived," said the mother of Lee Yong-ho, one of the airlifted survivors, as she waited in a Seoul hospital for her son.
"I felt as if my blood was drying up," she said.
Hong Duck-won, elder brother of the Korean-born American, told reporters his brother, Hong Hyun-seong, did not speak a word to him. "He just saw me in the eyes and held my hand firmly."
Hong Hyun-seong, who migrated to Guam in 1985 to run a Korean restaurant there, later told a local reporter: "I am sorry about the other passengers."
On Wednesday, he told a South Korean television that he pulled a female flight attendant to safety before he walked out of the wreckage but fire stopped him from rescuing trapped children.
"When I shouted into the wreckage asking whether anybody was alive, children shouted for help. I asked them 'how many' and they said 'four'," he said in the television interview.
"It was frustrating and unfortunate but I could not get back in because fire caused blasts inside the plane."
Doctors said none of the eight survivors faced serious danger of loss of life.

U.S. safety investigators searching through wreckage said it was too early to determine what caused the crash. In Washington, the National Transportation Safety Board said it had begun deciphering the information and date from the jet's flight data and voice recorders.
